hints: Look closely at cell P in the lower part of the image. How big is it compared to the many small grey cells around it, and what shape is its dark nucleus?
Recall that a lymphocyte has one large, round, dark-staining nucleus that fills almost the whole cell with only a thin rim of cytoplasm, unlike a lobed or kidney-shaped nucleus.
walkthrough:
**Observe what is in the picture**

First, notice the background. The very numerous small grey discs with no nucleus are red blood cells. The few larger cells with dark nuclei are white blood cells.

Cell P is slightly larger than a red blood cell and has a nucleus, so it must be a white blood cell.

**Focus on the nucleus of cell P**

Cell P has a single, large, round and very dark nucleus that fills almost the entire cell. There is only a very thin pale rim of cytoplasm around it.

This is the classic appearance of a lymphocyte.

**Compare with the other white cells**

Look at the other white cells in the image. Some have a nucleus divided into 3 to 4 dark lobes. Those are neutrophils. One cell near the top centre is larger with a paler, less dense nucleus. That fits a monocyte.

Cell P does not show lobes and is not large and pale, so A is the clear match.

options.A: Correct. Cell P shows a small white blood cell with a large round dense nucleus filling most of the cell, which is characteristic of a lymphocyte.
options.B: Not correct. A monocyte is larger with more cytoplasm and a paler, often kidney-shaped nucleus, not the small dark round nucleus seen in P.
options.C: Not correct. A neutrophil has a multi-lobed nucleus, like the cells with 3 to 4 dark lobes visible elsewhere in this image, which P does not have.
options.D: Not correct. Red blood cells are the small grey discs with no nucleus, while cell P clearly has a large dark nucleus.
